problem_text: Let p be an odd prime number, and let G be a finite group of order p(p + 1). Assume that G does not have a normal Sylow p-subgroup. Prove that p + 1 is a power of 2.
solution_text: Proof: (1) By Sylow's theorem, n_p | (p+1), n_p ≡ 1 (mod p), n_p > 1. Write n_p = kp+1. Since n_p | (p+1) and kp+1 ≤ p+1 with k≥1, we get k=1 so n_p = p+1. (2) |N_G(P)| = |G|/n_p = p(p+1)/(p+1) = p. Since P ⊆ N_G(P) and |P| = p, we have N_G(P) = P (self-normalizing). P is abelian (cyclic of prime order), so P ⊆ Z(N_G(P)) = Z(P) = P. (3) By Burnside's normal p-complement theorem, G has a normal p-complement N with |N| = p+1. (4) G = N ⋊ P. P acts on N by conjugation. The action is faithful: if P centralizes N, then G = N × P and P ◁ G, contradicting the hypothesis. (5) By orbit counting, |C_N(P)| ≡ |N| = p+1 ≡ 1 (mod p). Since the action is faithful, |C_N(P)| ≠ p+1, so |C_N(P)| = 1. The p non-identity elements form orbits of size p, giving exactly 1 orbit. All non-identity elements of N are conjugate under P, hence have the same order d. (6) d is prime: if d = ab with a,b > 1, then g^a has order b < d, contradiction. By Cauchy's theorem, no prime q ≠ d divides |N| (else an element of order q exists), so |N| = d^a = p+1. (7) If d is odd and a ≥ 2: p = d^a - 1 = (d-1)(d^{a-1} + d^{a-2} + ... + 1), which is composite since d-1 ≥ 2. If a = 1: p = d - 1 is even, contradicting p odd. Both cases contradict p being an odd prime. (8) Therefore d = 2, N is an elementary abelian 2-group, and p+1 = 2^a for some positive integer a.
solution_summary: Sylow counting gives n_p = p+1; self-normalizing abelian Sylow p-subgroup plus Burnside's normal p-complement theorem yields a normal subgroup N of order p+1; faithful conjugation action of P on N forces all non-identity elements to have the same prime order d; if d is odd, p = d^a - 1 factors nontrivially (or is even), contradicting primality of p; hence d = 2 and p+1 = 2^n.
answer: p + 1 = 2^n for some positive integer n
structure_features: Finite group of order p(p+1) with p odd prime, non-normal Sylow p-subgroup; requires bridging group-theoretic hypotheses to number-theoretic conclusion via normal p-complement theorem and conjugation action orbit analysis
key_objects: conjugation action of P on N
key_insight: All non-identity elements of the normal p-complement N have the same prime order d; if d is odd, then p = d^a - 1 = (d-1)(d^{a-1}+...+1) is composite (or even when a=1), contradicting p being an odd prime; hence d = 2 and p+1 = 2^a.

correct_method: Sylow counting to get n_p=p+1, Burnside's normal p-complement theorem for normal subgroup N, faithful conjugation action orbit analysis, arithmetic contradiction via factorization of d^a-1

Since N_G(P) = P and P is abelian, P ≤ Z(P) = P = Z(N_G(P)), so the theorem applies. G has a normal subgroup N of order p+1.

rounds.question: All non-identity elements of N have the same order d. Show d must be prime, determine |N| in terms of d, and derive a contradiction if d is odd.
rounds.expected_answer: d is prime: if d = ab with a,b > 1, then g^a has order b < d, contradicting all elements having order d. rounds.expected_answer: Since d = 2, N is an elementary abelian 2-group of order 2^a = p+1. Therefore p+1 is a power of 2, i.e., p+1 = 2^n for some positive integer n. QED.
